title: CDS Practice Set 10
pageDesc: Free CDS practice paper set 10 with detailed solutions. Pattern: English.

blueprint.name: English
blueprint.source: CDS Paper I English: 120 questions, 100 marks, 2 hours; negative 1/3.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom: "To blow one's own trumpet."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Visualize the literal imagery — blowing a trumpet creates loud noise to draw attention to oneself. Worked Solution: The idiom metaphorically means to boast or praise one's own abilities/achievements. Option A is opposite, B is literal, C is unrelated. Option D captures the figurative meaning of self-praise.

questions.text: Identify the segment containing the grammatical error: "No sooner did the teacher enter the class when the students stood up."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Correlative Conjunction Rule: 'No sooner' always pairs with 'than' (never 'when'). 'Hardly/Scarcely' pairs with 'when/before'. Inversion (Did + Subject) after 'No sooner' is correct. Step-by-step: 1. Sentence starts with negative adverbial 'No sooner' -> Inversion 'did the teacher enter' is correct. 2. Error is conjunction 'when'. 3. Standard pair is 'No sooner... than'. 4. Correction: 'No sooner did the teacher enter the class than the students stood up.'

questions.text: Improve the bracketed part of the sentence: 'He (not only came late but) forgot to bring his books.'

options.label: A
options.text: not only did he come late but also forgot

options.label: B
options.text: came not only late but also forgot

options.label: C
options.text: not only he came late but also forgot

options.label: D
options.text: not only came late but also forgot

questions.solution: Elimination Trick: Test Parallelism. The structure is 'Not only A but also B'. A and B must be grammatically similar (both verbs/verb phrases sharing the subject 'He'). Option A inverts subject-verb unnecessarily ('did he come'). Option B splits the verb 'came' from 'not only'. Option C inserts 'he' breaking the flow. Option D maintains perfect parallelism: 'He [not only came late] [but also forgot]'. Full Solution: Correlative conjunctions 'not only... but also' require parallel structure. Since the subject 'He' is common, the verbs 'came' and 'forgot' should follow 'not only' and 'but also' respectively. The original sentence misses 'also', making Option D the correct improvement.

questions.text: Change the following sentence into Passive Voice: "You must finish the work today."

options.label: A
options.text: The work must be finished by you today.

options.label: B
options.text: The work must finished by you today.

options.label: C
options.text: The work must be finish by you today.

options.label: D
options.text: The work is must finished by you today.

questions.solution: Shortcut: For Modal verbs (must, should, ought to) in Passive Voice, use the formula: Object + Modal + be + V3 + by + Subject. Step-by-step: 1. Identify Object ('the work'). 2. Keep Modal ('must'). 3. Add 'be' + Past Participle of main verb ('be finished'). 4. Add 'by' + Subject ('by you'). 5. Retain adverbial ('today'). Result: 'The work must be finished by you today.'

questions.text: Choose the word which best expresses the meaning: "A place where birds are kept."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Use root-word elimination. 'Avi-' (Latin 'avis') = bird; 'Api-' = bee; 'Aqua-' = water. Worked Solution: 'Apiary' is for bees, 'Aquarium' for aquatic life, 'Sanctuary' is a general refuge. 'Aviary' specifically denotes a large enclosure for keeping birds.

questions.text: Improve the bracketed part of the sentence: "If he (would have studied) harder, he would have passed the exam."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Third Conditional (Unreal Past) Rule: 'If' clause never uses 'would have'. Structure: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), ... would have + V3. Step-by-step: 1. Sentence describes hypothetical past result. 2. 'Would have studied' is grammatically incorrect inside 'If' clause. 3. Correct tense for 'If' clause is Past Perfect: 'had studied'. 4. Main clause 'would have passed' is already correct. Result: 'If he had studied harder...'

questions.text: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate phrasal verb: "The police promised to ______ the allegations of corruption."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Match context keywords. 'Allegations' + 'Police' = Investigation. 'Look into' = Investigate. Worked Solution: 'Look after' means care for; 'look up' means search/improve; 'look down upon' means despise. Only 'look into' fits the context of an official inquiry into allegations.

questions.text: Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error: 'The economics of the proposed project are very complicated for a layman to understand.'
questions.solution: Elimination Trick: Identify the subject ('Economics') – it is a noun plural in form but singular in meaning (denoting a field of study), like Mathematics, Physics, or News. Such subjects always take a singular verb. Option C ('are') is a plural verb, creating a Subject-Verb Agreement error. The correct verb is 'is'. Full Solution: The subject 'Economics' refers to the academic discipline/science, which is singular. Therefore, the verb must be singular ('is'). Segment C contains the error.

questions.text: Change the narration: He said to me, "Please don't open the door."

options.label: A
options.text: He ordered me to not open the door.

options.label: B
options.text: He requested me not to open the door.

options.label: C
options.text: He asked me that I should not open the door.

options.label: D
options.text: He told me please don't open the door.

questions.solution: Shortcut: Imperative sentences with 'Please' change Reporting Verb to 'requested/advised'. Negative 'don't' becomes 'not to'. Remove inverted commas. Step-by-step: 1. 'Said to' becomes 'requested' (due to 'Please'). 2. 'Me' remains object. 3. 'Don't open' converts to 'not to open' (Infinitive negative). 4. Pronouns unchanged. Result: 'He requested me not to open the door.'

questions.text: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate preposition: 'The manager did not agree ______ my proposal for the new marketing strategy.'
questions.solution: Elimination Trick: Apply the 'Agree' rule shortcut. 'Agree WITH' takes a person/entity (I agree with you). 'Agree TO' takes a proposal, plan, suggestion, or request (I agree to the plan). 'Agree ON' takes a topic/issue (We agree on the date). Here the object is 'my proposal' (a plan/suggestion). Options A, B, D are incorrect collocations for 'proposal'. Full Solution: The verb 'agree' collocates differently based on the object. When the object is a proposal, suggestion, or plan, the correct preposition is 'to'. Since 'proposal' is a plan put forward for consideration, 'agree to' is the standard usage.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom: 'To burn the midnight oil.'

options.label: A
options.text: To work late into the night

questions.solution: Elimination Trick: Visualize the literal imagery – burning oil in a lamp at midnight. Historically, this was done to study or work when daylight was gone. Option B, C, and D do not align with this historical context of studious effort. Option A captures the metaphorical meaning perfectly. Full Solution: The idiom originates from the time before electric lights when people used oil lamps to read or work late at night. It means to work or study hard, especially late into the night.

questions.text: Choose the word which best expresses the meaning of the given phrase: 'A person who hates mankind.'
questions.solution: Elimination Trick: Break down the roots. 'Anthropos' = mankind/human. 'Miso' = hatred. 'Gyne' = woman. 'Phil' = love. Option A (Philanthropist) loves mankind. Option C (Misogynist) hates women. Option D (Ascetic) practices self-denial. Option B (Misanthrope) combines Miso + Anthropos = hatred of mankind. Full Solution: 'Misanthrope' is the precise one-word substitution for a person who dislikes and avoids human society. The root 'anthropos' refers to humans/humanity, and 'mis-' indicates hatred.

questions.text: Identify the segment which contains the grammatical error: "Neither the captain nor the players was happy with the referee's decision."
questions.solution: Shortcut: Apply the Proximity Rule — with 'Neither...nor' / 'Either...or', the verb agrees with the noun/pronoun nearest to it (here, 'players', plural). Worked Solution: The subjects are 'captain' (singular) and 'players' (plural) joined by 'nor'. The verb must agree with the closer subject 'players', requiring plural 'were'. Segment C uses singular 'was', hence the error.

questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Ubiquitous'.
questions.solution: Shortcut: Root 'Ubi-' (Latin: everywhere). Eliminate antonyms (Rare) and unrelated distractors (Confusing, Ambiguous). Step-by-step: 1. 'Ubiquitous' means existing everywhere simultaneously. 2. 'Omnipresent' (Omni=all, present) is the direct synonym. 3. 'Rare' is antonym. 4. 'Confusing/Ambiguous' relate to clarity, not presence. Correct: Omnipresent.

questions.text: Improve the bracketed part of the sentence: "It is high time that we (leave) this place immediately."
questions.solution: Shortcut: The structure 'It is high time / It is time' is always followed by Simple Past (V2) to indicate present/future necessity (Subjunctive mood). Worked Solution: 'Leave' is base form (V1), 'left' is Simple Past (V2). The sentence expresses current urgency, so 'left' is grammatically correct. 'Have left' (Present Perfect) and 'had left' (Past Perfect) are structurally incorrect here.
